facts.claim: The 1978 adaptation study included 22 major lottery winners, 22 controls, and 29 people paralyzed in accidents.
facts.mechanism: Because Comparing extreme positive and negative changes with a control group allowed the researchers to test whether contrast and adaptation altered everyday pleasure and reported happiness.
facts.commonError: The famous study followed thousands of participants for many years.
facts.whyWrong: It was a small cross-sectional comparison with the stated group sizes.

facts.claim: The lottery winners and accident victims did not converge to an identical level of well-being in the 1978 data.
facts.mechanism: Because Adaptation reduced contrasts without erasing the enduring burden associated with paralysis.
facts.commonError: Lottery winners and paralyzed accident survivors became equally happy after enough time.
facts.whyWrong: That retelling overstates what the group comparisons showed.

facts.claim: The sustainable-happiness model distinguishes set-point influences, circumstances, and intentional activities.
facts.mechanism: Because The categories separate relatively stable disposition, environmental conditions, and repeated chosen behavior as different sources of variation.
facts.commonError: The model claims happiness has only one controllable cause.
facts.whyWrong: It explicitly includes three classes of influence.

facts.claim: The popular 50-10-40 happiness percentages should not be applied as fixed causal shares for an individual.
facts.mechanism: Because Population estimates depend on measurement and context, interact with each other, and do not partition one person's well-being like a budget.
facts.commonError: Exactly 40 percent of anyone's happiness can be changed by voluntary activity.
facts.whyWrong: The numerical allocation is a heuristic derived from heterogeneous research, not an individual diagnostic equation.

facts.claim: Flow is most likely when perceived challenge and skill are both high and reasonably matched.
facts.mechanism: Because The match demands full attention without making success feel impossible or the task trivial.
facts.commonError: Flow is simple relaxation in an easy activity.
facts.whyWrong: Low challenge tends toward boredom or passive pleasure rather than deep absorption.

facts.claim: Clear goals and prompt feedback help sustain flow.
facts.mechanism: Because They keep attention coupled to the next task-relevant adjustment instead of to self-monitoring.
facts.commonError: Any difficult task creates flow automatically.
facts.whyWrong: Difficulty without legible goals or feedback more often produces confusion and anxiety.

facts.claim: Longer commuting time has been associated with lower life satisfaction in German panel data.
facts.mechanism: Because Time loss, low control, and repeated travel stress can recur more reliably than compensating benefits enter daily awareness.
facts.commonError: People fully adapt to commuting because they voluntarily chose the job and home tradeoff.
facts.whyWrong: The commuting paradox is that predicted compensation was incomplete in reported satisfaction.

facts.claim: Hedonic adaptation varies across life events and conditions rather than following one universal timetable.
facts.mechanism: Because Events differ in novelty, recurrence, attention, control, and the goals they continue to obstruct.
facts.commonError: Every gain or loss fades completely after a standard number of months.
facts.whyWrong: Longitudinal findings show heterogeneous and sometimes incomplete adaptation.

facts.claim: Spending can support well-being when it improves security, time use, relationships, or meaningful experience rather than status comparison alone.
facts.mechanism: Because Those uses change repeated daily conditions or social connection, while positional gains invite comparison and adaptation.
facts.commonError: Money never affects happiness once basic survival is covered.
facts.whyWrong: Income and spending choices can alter real conditions even though their marginal benefits diminish.
